clips.title: HashiCorp Vault Tutorial for Beginners - What, Why and How
clips.why: Nana shows how secrets spread when every team keeps them in its own place, which is exactly what the shortcut in the story would have started.
look: Secrets copied into config files, CI tools and environment variables, until nobody knows where all the copies are.
The two big problems of that sprawl: you cannot see who has access, and you cannot rotate a key everywhere at once.
Why one central store with access rules and an audit log answers both.
clips.after: Vault on inf is that central store. The GitHub App key has one home, infrastructure/ai-agents/broker, and every copy is made from there by an ExternalSecret.

clips.title: External Secrets Operator Explained (ESO) | Kubernetes Secrets Made Simple
clips.why: A short, recent explanation of what the External Secrets operator does and the four steps to use it. The speaker uses his own company's secret store; ours is Vault, and the steps are the same.
look: Why native Kubernetes Secrets alone are a problem: base64 and copies managed by hand.
The operator syncs from an outside store into normal Kubernetes Secrets, so applications do not change.
The four steps: install the operator, give it a way to log in, create a store, create an ExternalSecret.
clips.after: In the lab you do the same four steps with Vault, and the login you give the store decides what it may read.

clips.title: HashiCorp Vault + Kubernetes: Create External Secrets
clips.why: The last mile: a pod reading the synced Secret as environment variables.
look: The Deployment refers to the Secret by name; it never talks to Vault.
The values arrive in the container as ordinary environment variables.
Think about when the process reads them: only once, at start.
clips.after: The broker's pod reads GITHUB_APP_KEY the same way, which is why a rotated key needs a restart to reach the running process.

practice.q: A teammate wants to put the Slack bot token in the unit's env block "just for the first deploy". How many places would hold a copy?

options.why: The repo is only the first copy. The plan, the Terraform state and Helm's release record hold it too.

options.text: Four: git history, the pasted plan, the Terraform state and Helm's release record in the cluster
options.why: And none of them can be cleaned up reliably. The only fix after that is to rotate the token.

options.text: None, because Terraform hides values marked sensitive
options.why: Marking a value sensitive hides it in plan output, but it is still in git and in the state file in plain text.

practice.q: Finish the command so the key comes from stdin and never appears on the command line.
practice.before: printf '%s' "$key" | vault kv put -mount=kvv2 infrastructure/ai-agents/broker GITHUB_APP_KEY=
practice.hint: One character that means "read the value from the input stream".
practice.why: =- tells Vault to read the value from stdin, so it never shows in the shell history or in the process list.

practice.q: Finish the Vault policy so the store for ai-agents can read our folder and nothing else.
practice.hint: Our folder name, then a wildcard.
practice.why: kvv2/data/infrastructure/ai-agents/* covers every secret of the agent platform and nothing of n8n or any other tool.

practice.q: Put the journey of a rotated key in order.
items: A person writes the new key into Vault from stdin, which creates version 2
Within one refresh interval, the operator reads the path through the store's login
The operator updates the Kubernetes Secret in ai-agents
The Deployment is restarted, so new pods read the new value at start
The broker uses the new key
practice.why: The operator moves the value as far as the Secret by itself. A process that reads environment variables only sees it after a restart.

practice.q: Which object decides whether an ExternalSecret may copy n8n's password?

options.why: The ExternalSecret only asks. Anyone who can write one can ask for anything.
Vault knows nothing about Kubernetes namespaces. It only knows which login is asking.

options.text: The store's Vault login and its policy
options.why: Vault checks the login's policy on every read. That is why a store of our own with a narrow policy is the real wall.
